idiom_name: one struct implementing both traits; Rc<RefCell<_>> with a Weak back-link only if two addressable ends are required
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance: behaviour is shared by implementing traits, and a type may implement any number of them, so a single struct can be a GameItem and a Tickable at the same time - the twin's two-object split is only needed when two runtimes must each own an addressable value. Where that is genuinely required, mutual Rc<RefCell<_>> references are a documented leak (the book's reference-cycle chapter: 'it's possible to create references where items refer to each other in a cycle ... the values will never be dropped'), so the back-link must be a Weak obtained through Rc::downgrade - or the ownership reorganised so only one direction owns. Trait upcasting, stable since Rust 1.86, removes the old workaround of writing as_supertrait() methods when one trait object must be seen through a supertrait.
pitfalls: Mutual Rc<RefCell<_>> links leak: each side keeps the other's strong count above zero and the compiler cannot catch it - use Rc::downgrade/Weak for one direction (Rc::new_cyclic hands out a Weak self-reference during construction) or keep ownership one-way.

Two objects calling each other must take RefCell borrows on both sides; a crossing call that re-enters while a borrow_mut is live panics at runtime, because RefCell enforces the borrowing rules dynamically.
Split state must be shared explicitly: a field needed by both ends belongs in one end or in a shared Rc<RefCell<_>>/Arc<Mutex<_>>; duplicating it makes the two ends disagree.

Splitting one logical entity into two types doubles the threading problem: each end must be Send/Sync on its own (Arc<Mutex<_>> rather than Rc<RefCell<_>>) as soon as either end moves to another thread.
